newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran seeks better Gulf ties, but road choppy.
newsitem.headline: Iran seeks better Gulf ties, but road choppy.

text.p: Iran is actively seeking friendly ties with its Arab neighbours across the Gulf, but the Islamic republic has a long and choppy way to go to restore trust with Gulf Arab states, analysts and officials said on Thursday.

The main message Iran's Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati carried with him when he visited the six Gulf states this week was that Iran does not pose a regional threat and has no aggressive intentions against its neighbours, they said.

"How convincing he was is still to be seen," one Gulf official said. "There are very complex problems that need to be addressed and the Iranians know this. But this tour might be just the first step."
"Iran is working hard for an accommodation with its neighbours especially Saudi Arabia," said a diplomat in Tehran.

Relations with Saudi Arabia, the most influential Gulf country and custodian to Islam's two holiest shrines, have been tense since Iran's 1979 revolution and as usual are further strained before the annual haj pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina.

While insisting that political rallies should be held during the haj in defiance of a Saudi ban, speeches by Tehran leaders have been less virulent than the past years and they have also stressed the need to preserve Moslem unity, an Iranian analyst said.
The analyst said Tehran's desire to improve ties with Riyadh have been reflected by a softer tone used by the media and officials towards Saudi Arabia in the past few weeks.

"The Iranians have doubled attempts at improving ties with Saudi Arabia since the Khobar bombing because they believe Washington is pressuring the Saudis to blame Tehran and provide the U.S. with an excuse to attack Iran," he added.
Riyadh has refused to confirm U.S. media reports of an Iranian link to the June bombing which killed 19 U.S. servicemen in the eastern Saudi city of Khobar.
Iran -- which Washington accuses of sponsoring state terrorism and has imposed sanctions on -- denies any role.
Velayati said that his visit to Saudi Arabia had opened up a new chapter in relations between Tehran and Riyadh.

He urged reporters in Kuwait to ask regional Arab states "'do you feel any threat from Iran'. I have not heard, specifically during recent weeks and months, from the people in this region that they feel some threat from Iran."
"Neighbouring countries feel that Iran is much more cooperative and from the other side we...say that 'We are not looking for conflict or (regional) superiority'," said Velayati.

Both Shi'ite Moslem Iran and the Sunni Moslem leaders of the Gulf Arab states are aware that maintaining the delicate stability in a region that sits on 45 percent of the world's oil reserves is a must, the officials and diplomats said.
But the murky road to trust is complex.

The six Gulf Cooperation Council states -- Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Oman, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates -- still view with concern Iran's arms programme and still see it interfering in their internal affairs.
Iran denies it interferes in its neighbours' internal affairs and says its arms programme is for defence purposes.

Iran also has to settle a territorial dispute with the UAE, the only Gulf state where Velayati -- who delivered invitations to a December summit in Tehran of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference (OIC) -- did not meet the head of state.

Arab diplomats said an Iranian request for an audience with President Sheikh Zaid bin Sultan al-Nahayan was turned down. Velayati delivered the invitation to Prince Sultan, the UAE's deputy prime minister and a son of Sheikh Zaid.

Iran lost goodwill in the region when it upset the status quo by flexing its military muscle in 1992 on the island of Abu Musa, which it shares with the UAE, provoking Abu Dhabi to revive its claim to two other islands seized by Iran in 1971.

Velayati reiterated on his tour his country's opposition to the presence of U.S. and Western forces in the volatile area bristling with the world's most sophisticated conventional weaponry and said security was a regional responsibility.
Arab diplomats said Velayati received a "less than enthusiastic" reception in Bahrain, which last year accused Iran of links to a plot to topple the government. Iran denied that.
